items.why: Tests the negation contrasting unchanged conduct with renewed priest appointments.
The unanchored 'he' and awkward 'message ... happen' obscure the intended speaker contrast.
Separates Jonathan’s individual victory from the collective attribution to David and his men.
Requires tracking the officer through the prophecy and its fulfillment.
Distinguishes the father who rides from the sons who saddle the donkey.
Distinguishes the first covenant’s three parties from the later two-party covenant.
The succession answer is clear, but Isaiah’s recording provides a weak competing sequence.
Separates Uzziah’s stated reason for leaving from the priests’ action.
Treats the king’s conjecture as the Arameans’ actual expectation.
Distinguishes their chosen surrender from the rejected option of entering the city.
Asks for incidental kill order across separate battles rather than a meaningful event contrast.
The key merely says 'the news' without identifying what was reported.
The target is clear, but the king ordering his own capture is an implausible rival.
The question itself makes Azariah implausible as the person Azariah follows.
Requires tracking whose child 'my son' identifies inside the reported proposal.
Separates Zechariah’s instruction from Amaziah’s example.
Distinguishes the reply from the initial prophecy, though the key leaves 'he' unnamed.
Tests obedience to God rather than treating a hypothetical gift as the cause.
Uses an explicit temporal clause to distinguish continued talking from the earlier meal.
Selecting the first action in an explicit three-verb sequence offers limited discrimination.
Distinguishes the weapons’ distributor from their former owner.
The answer is explicit, while 'the addressee' makes the question unnecessarily formal.
'Take Amaziah’s son' is an unnatural way to describe the people’s choice of king.
Resolves 'their command' while distinguishing military leaders from mustering officials.
Tracks the subject shift from the prophet saddling the donkey to the man of God departing.
Duplicates the officer-trampling question tested more strongly by Q89C41.
The supplied wording orders both groups to guard the temple, making the key incomplete.
Cleanly distinguishes the letter’s sender from its named recipient.
Connects 'the Philistine' to Ishbi-Benob rather than to the man Abishai rescues.
Contrasts their decision to report the news with their earlier concealment of loot.
Distinguishes the young informant from Paul, who arranges his access to the commander.
Tests the transition from the messengers’ report to the people’s plundering.
'Love of soil explains the farm work' makes a clear causal-reference question sound contrived.
Resolves 'my son' as the reporting woman’s child rather than the other woman’s hidden child.
Clearly separates requester from intercessor, but the praying agent is explicitly repeated.
Requires all three opponents and distinguishes them from the tribute-paying Ammonites.
The city and its tomb are nested destinations, not clearly separate first and second stops.
The nested possessive is awkward, and the competing answer names someone explicitly dead.
Distinguishes the stated cause of calm from the people’s simultaneous rejoicing.
Separates the officers receiving the order from the troops they must assemble.
Distinguishes the imagined attackers from the king believed to have hired them.
Identifies the sender condemned as a murderer, not the messenger sent to kill.
Tracks the intended guest through the prophet’s claimed angelic instruction.
The reason is explicit, and the lamps provide no plausible competing cause.
Tracks the split between soldiers returning and cavalry continuing with Paul.
Tracks 'they' back to Sceva’s sons rather than the man who attacked them.
Illnesses also disappear; the distinction hinges on wording rather than different outcomes.
Separates the commander asked to transfer Paul from the council requesting him.
Generic 'assembling materials' obscures the concrete act of gathering their scrolls.
Tests the explicit sword order’s target rather than the woman’s separate execution.
Distinguishes what draws Athaliah to the temple from what she sees after arriving.
The vague 'act' does not clearly distinguish consent from Paul’s transfer as a prerequisite.
The malformed 'whose body is warned' makes an otherwise clear referent question unnatural.
Distinguishes the prophesied Josiah from Jeroboam, who is currently at the altar.
